STATEMENT OF THE ASSIGNMENTS OF ERROR PRESENTED FOR REVIEW

DENIED PLAINTIFFS-APPELLANTS' MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT, AS NO GENUINE ISSUE OF MATERIAL FACT EXISTED AND TRAVELERS WAS ENTITLED TO JUDGMENT IN ITS FAVOR AS A MATTER OF LAW.
II. THE TRIAL COURT, IN ITS MAY 15, 2008 JOURNAL ENTRY, CORRECTLY DENIED APPELLANTS' MOTION FOR RELIEF FROM JUDGMENT PURSUANT TO CIV.R. 60(B) BECAUSE APPELLANTS' MOTION MERELY SOUGHT RECONSIDERATION OF THE TRIAL COURT'S DECISION TO GRANT TRAVELERS' MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT.

STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES PRESENTED FOR REVIEW
I. Whether Appellee's insured, Prime TV LLC ("Prime"), effectively released Appellee from any liability pursuant to the insurance policy Appellee issued (the "Policy") with respect to claims of the type that form the basis of the judgment that Appellants later obtained against Prime (the "Judgment")? (Assignment Of Error I)
II. Whether Appellants, as judgment creditors, are "standing in the shoes" of Prime, with no greater rights than Prime, and subject to any defenses that Appellee would have against a claim by Prime? (Assignment Of Error I)
III. Whether Appellants are third-party beneficiaries under the Policy? (Assignment Of Error I)
IV. Whether R.C. §3929.05 applies to cases that involve neither the cancellation of an insurance policy nor claims for "bodily injury" caused by an "accident," notwithstanding its clear terms? (Assignment Of Error I)
V. Whether the terms of the Policy barred Prime from releasing Appellee? (Assignment Of Error I)
VI. Whether Prime's sending of unsolicited facsimile advertisements to Appellants constitutes the "advertising injury" offense of "oral or written publication of material that violates a persons right of privacy" under the Policy? (Assignment Of Error I)
VII. Whether the exclusion in the Policy for injury "arising out of the willful violation of a penal statute" bars coverage for the Judgment because it was premised on a finding that Prime "knowingly and willfully" sent Appellants unsolicited facsimile advertisements in violation of 47 U.S.C. §227, which is a crime pursuant to 47 U.S.C. §§501, 503(b)? (Assignment Of Error I)
VIII. Whether Ohio public policy precludes insurance coverage for intentionally caused injuries such as those that form the basis of the Judgment? (Assignment Of Error I)
IX. Whether Appellee is entitled to conduct discovery regarding facts relevant to whether the Judgment was the result of fraud or collusion and the applicability of the exclusion in the Policy for injury "arising out of oral or written publication of material whose first publication took place before the beginning of the policy period"? (Assignment Of Error I)
X. Whether it is an abuse of discretion for a trial court to deny a motion brought pursuant to Civ.R. 60(B) when the motion seeks only reconsideration of the merits of a final judgment issued by the trial court? (Assignment Of Error II)

STATEMENT OF THE CASE
The trial court held that Appellant-Defendant Travelers Indemnity Company ("Travelers") was entitled to summary judgment because it received a full release in connection with Appellants' claims. In a separate suit, Appellants obtained a judgment against Travelers' insured, Prime TV, LLC ("Prime"), based on a finding that Prime "knowingly and willfully" sent Appellants unsolicited fax advertisements in violation of the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, 47 U.S.C. §227 (the "TCPA"). In this case, Appellants claim Travelers must pay that judgment on behalf of Prime pursuant to an insurance policy Travelers issued to Prime. Travelers raised various defenses, including that it has no duty to pay the judgment on behalf of Prime because, long before Appellants obtained the judgment, Prime released Travelers from any liability under the policy with respect to claims of the type Appellants asserted against Prime.
The trial court instructed the parties to file motions for summary judgment regarding the release issue only. Travelers did so, but Appellants filed a motion regarding all issues in the case. In response, Travelers asserted several of its defenses, including that it had no duty to pay the judgment because: (1) Prime released Travelers; (2) the policy affords no coverage for the damages awarded in the judgment; and (3) public policy bars coverage for damages awarded against an insured that intentionally caused injury. Alternatively, Travelers requested time pursuant to Civ.R. 56(F) to conduct the discovery needed to brief its other defenses.
The trial court granted Travelers' motion and denied Appellants' motion, holding that Travelers has no duty to pay the judgment on behalf of Prime because Prime released Travelers. The trial court reasoned that the only rights that Appellants, as judgment creditors, possess against Travelers are those possessed by Prime at the time Appellants obtained the judgment and concluded that, because Prime had no rights against Travelers, Appellants have no rights against

Travelers. Therefore, the court did not address Travelers' other defenses. The court later denied Appellants' Civ.R. 60(B) motion, which asked the court to "reconsider and reverse" its holding.
Appellants appealed the trial court's order denying their motion and granting Travelers' motion and the order denying their Civ.R. 60(B) motion. The orders should be affirmed because they are correct in all respects and because, even absent the release Travelers received from Prime, Travelers was entitled to summary judgment based on its other defenses.
STATEMENT OF FACTS
A. The TCPA
The TCPA bans unsolicited facsimile advertisements ("fax ads"), creates a private right of action in the recipient of such fax ads, and provides for statutory damages of $500 per unsolicited fax ad. 47 U.S.C. §227(b)(1)(C), (b)(3).1 In addition, the TCPA permits a plaintiff to recover treble damages of $1,500 per fax if the defendant willfully violated the TCPA. 47 U.S.C. §227(b)(3). A willful violation of the TCPA is a crime punishable by a fine of up to $10,000 and/or up to one year in prison for a first offense and up to two years in prison for a second offense. 47 U.S.C. §501. One who willfully violates the TCPA is also liable for a "forfeiture penalty" of up to $10,000 per violation. 47 U.S.C. §503(b).

Prime TV, LLC, Case No. 05-CV-553459, Court of Common Pleas of Cuyahoga County, based on a finding that it was "undisputed that [Prime] knowingly and willfully violated [the TCPA] by transmitting, to the [Appellants], the

C. The Travelers Policy
Travelers issued to Prime Policy No. I-680-371D839-4-IND-00, with an effective period of September 25, 2000 to September 25, 2001 (the "Policy"). (Id., 16). The Policy provides: "We will pay those sums that the insured becomes legally obligated to pay as damages because of ... 'advertising injury' to which this insurance applies" and that "[t]his insurance applies to: . . . '[a]dvertising injury' caused by an offense committed in the course of advertising. . . . " (Id., 17). The Policy also provides: "This insurance does not apply to: ... 'advertising injury': ... (2) Arising out of oral or written publication of material whose first publication took place before the beginning of the policy period; [or] (3) Arising out of the willful violation of a penal statute or ordinance committed by or with the consent of the insured[.]" (Id., 18). The Policy defines "adverting injury" to mean injury arising out of one or more of the following offenses: "a. oral or written publication of material that slanders or libels a person . . .; b. oral or written publication of material that violates a person's right of privacy; c. Misappropriation of advertising ideas . . .; or d. infringement of copyright, title or slogan." (Id., 19).

D. Prime Released Travelers From Any Liability Pursuant To The Policy With Respect To TCPA Claims Against Prime
Effective as of April 14, 2005,2 Travelers and Prime entered into a Confidential Settlement Agreement And Mutual Release (the "Agreement") that fully and finally resolved a dispute between them regarding what coverage, if any, the Policy afforded for claims based on Prime's alleged sending of unsolicited fax ads. (Opp. Aff., 110). Pursuant to the Agreement, Prime released Travelers from any liability pursuant to the Policy in connection with such claims in exchange for a payment by Travelers toward the settlement of a class action against Prime based on TCPA claims. (Id., 111, Ex. C). The Agreement provides:
Prime releases . . . Travelers from all past, present and future actions, claims, .... or liabilities of any kind or nature, known or unknown, foreseen or unforeseen, matured or unmatured, under the Travelers Policies . .. which in any manner or fashion arise from or relate to: (i) the Class Settlement .. .; (ii) the Coverage Action .. .; and (iii) ... any and all past, present or future claims of any of the Potential Claimants.
(Id., (12). The Agreement defines: (1) "Class Settlement" to mean the settlement between Prime and the class of plaintiffs asserting TCPA claims against Prime; (2) "Coverage Action" to mean the litigation between Prime and Travelers regarding whether the Policy applied to TCPA claims; (3) "Potential Claimants" to mean "any and all individuals nationwide who ever received an allegedly unsolicited facsimile from Prime"; and (4) "Travelers Policies" to include the Policy. SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
Appellants ask this Court to ignore established Ohio law that limits the rights of judgment creditors to those possessed by the party against whom they obtained a judgment and hold instead that Appellants' rights far exceed those of Prime. No basis exists for such a radical departure from clear Ohio law.
The trial court correctly held that Travelers was entitled to judgment as a matter of law that it has no obligation to pay the Judgment because Prime released Travelers from any liability under the Policy with respect to claims such as those Appellants asserted against Prime. Under settled Ohio law, Appellants, as judgment creditors "standing in the shoes" of Prime, can assert only those rights possessed by Prime and any defenses that Travelers would have to a claim by Prime are valid against Appellants' claims. Because Prime long ago settled with and released Travelers, Prime has no rights against Travelers. Thus, Appellants have no rights against Travelers. Moreover, Ohio law is clear that injured persons have no vested rights in an insurance policy unless and until they obtain a judgment against the insured. At the time Prime released Travelers, Appellants had no vested rights in the Policy because Appellants did not obtain the Judgment until long after Prime and Travelers reached their settlement. Thus, "if an insured intentionally inflicts an injury, then as a matter of public policy, the contract of insurance would not afford coverage to such an act." Kish v. Cent. Nat'l Ins. Group (1981), 67 Ohio St.2d 41, 45 n.4, 424 N.E.2d 288 (citation and quotations omitted). See also Doe v. Shaffer (2000), 90 Ohio St.3d 388, 391, 738 N.E.2d 1243 ("As early as 1938, ... it was 'well settled from the standpoint of public policy that the act of intentionally inflicting an injury cannot be covered by insurance . .
- 35 -

. . ") (citation omitted); Buckeye Union Ins. Co. v. New England Ins. Co. (1999), 87 Ohio St.3d 280, 283, 720 N.E.2d 495 (public policy bars insurance coverage when the insured "does something which brings about the exact result desired"). Without such a rule, "the presence of insurance would encourage those who deliberately harm another." Harasyn v. Normandy Metals (1990), 49 Ohio St.3d 173, 177, 551 N.E.2d 962. See also Doe, 90 Ohio St.3d at 391, 738 N.E.2d 1243 ("such conduct would be encouraged if insurance were available to shift the financial cost of the loss from the wrongdoer to his insurer") (quotations and citation omitted); Gearing, 76 Ohio St.3d at 39, 665 N.E.2d 1115 ("requiring an insurer to indemnify an insured who has engaged in sexual abuse of a child subsidizes the episodes of sexual abuse of which its victims complain, at the ultimate expense of other insureds to whom the added costs of indemnifying child molesters will be passed").
Based on this settled principle of Ohio law, Travelers has no duty to pay the Judgment because it is premised exclusively on intentionally caused injuries. The only injuries at issue in the underlying action were Appellants' receipt of unsolicited fax ads. The Judgment is premised on the fact that Prime willfully sent those ads to Appellants knowing that they were unsolicited. Thus, Prime did something that brought about the exact result desired: It sent unsolicited fax ads to Appellants intending that Appellants' would receive them and that is exactly what happened. Accordingly, Ohio public policy bars coverage. See Buckeye, 87 Ohio St.3d at 283; Doe, 90 Ohio St.3d at 391. See also ACS Sys, Inc. v. St. Paul Fire & Marine Ins. Co. (Cal. Misc. 2005), Case No. BC 305455 ("the Court also finds merit in defendant's argument that allowing insurance coverage to cover costs of defense and to reimburse any civil or administrative penalties for this conduct [i.e., sending unsolicited fax ads]-which is expressly prohibited by federal law-would be a violation of public policy"), affd. on other grounds, (2007), 147 Cal.App.4th 137.
- 36 -

Significantly, if public policy did not bar coverage here, it would encourage companies such as Prime to continue deliberately sending unsolicited fax ads because they would be allowed to shift the financial cost of their willful violation of the TCPA to their insurers while retaining the financial benefit of their unlawful conduct. See Harasyn, 49 Ohio St.3d at 177; Doe, 90 Ohio St.3d at 391. Requiring insurers to indemnify those who intentionally violate the TCPA subsidizes the violations of which individuals such as Appellants complain, at the ultimate expense of other insureds to whom the costs of indemnifying blast-faxers will be passed. Public policy does not permit that result. See Gearing, 76 Ohio St.3d at 39.
2. Public Policy Bars Coverage For Treble Damages
Public policy does not permit insurance coverage for the treble damages awarded to the Appellants in the Judgment. Ohio public policy bars indemnification for punitive damages. See Ruffin v. Sawchyn (1991), 75 Ohio App.3d 511, 518, 599 N.E.2d 852 ("punitive damages are not insurable"). Where public policy bars indemnification for punitive damages, it likewise bars coverage for treble damages imposed upon an insured for willful misconduct.
In Casey v. Calhoun (1987), 40 Ohio App.3d 83, 84, 531 N.E.2d 1348, the court explained that "[p]unitive damages are awarded to punish an offender for the wanton, reckless, malicious or oppressive character of the act committed and to deter others from committing similar acts" and that "both the legislature and judiciary have determined that insuring against punitives is detrimental to the welfare and the morals of the public." The treble damages available for willful violations of the TCPA are indistinguishable from punitive damages:
The TCPA gives the court discretion to increase damages up to three times for willful or knowing violations of the statute. Treble damages, historically were to guard against unscrupulous business practices and conduct that constitutes willful and knowing violations of existing laws. Treble damages are a form of punitive damages, the purpose of which are to punish the person or entity doing the wrongful act and to discourage that person or entity from similar conduct in the
- 37 -

future. See Texas Industries, Inc. v. Radcliff Materials, Inc., 451 U.S. 630, 639, 68 L. Ed. 2d 500, 101 S. Ct. 2061 (1981).
Covington & Burling v. Int'l Mktg. & Research, Inc. (D.C.Super.Ct., Apr. 17, 2003), 2003 D.C. Super. LEXIS 29, at *23 -* 26. Public policy bars insurance for treble damages awarded under the TCPA because they serve the same purposes as punitive damages. In a similar situation, the court in Rental & Mgmt. Assocs. v. Hartford Ins. Co. (N.Y. Misc. 1992), 588 N.Y.S.2d 982, affd. (App.Div. 1994), 614 N.Y.S.2d 513, held that public policy barred coverage for treble damages awarded against landlords for wrongful evictions. The court explained:
Damages ... are trebled in order to punish and deter. ... Clearly the Legislature intended to compound the damages in order to discourage resort to wrongful evictions by landlords and to punish severely those who engage in such conduct. . . The damages are a reflection of ethical indignation and a sort of fine. Allowing insurance coverage would weaken the deterrent and water down the punishment. Further, it would be unjust, perhaps even absurd, to allow a landlord to pass on to its insurance company, to say nothing of other purchasers of insurance, part of the punishment intended for it.
Id. at 982. Therefore, of the $87,000 awarded to the Appellants in the Judgment, public policy bars Travelers from paying at least the $58,000 that was awarded as treble damages.
E. Travelers Is Entitled To Conduct Discovery
It is not clear whether Appellants and Prime entered into some sort of agreement that resulted in the Judgment or whether the Judgment was otherwise the result of fraud or collusion. An insurer has no duty to indemnify an insured for a settlement or judgment that results from fraud or collusion between the insured and the underlying plaintiffs. See Stoller v. Fid. & Guar. Ins. Underwriters (Aug. 5, 1988), 1988 Ohio App. LEXIS 3097, at *17. Discovery may reveal facts that will establish that the Judgment is the result of fraud or collusion between Appellants and Prime.
- 38 -

Discovery may likewise reveal that coverage for the Judgment is barred by the Policy's exclusion for injury "arising out of oral or written publication of material whose first publication took place before the beginning of the policy period." Where an insured publishes an ad within a coverage period that is substantially the same as one it published prior to the coverage period, the "first publication" exclusion bars coverage for any injury arising from the ad published during the term of the policy. See, e.g., Hedarina v. Chubb Group of Ins. Cos. (9th Cir., Aug. 26, 1998), 1998 U.S. App. LEXIS 21103, *8; Applied Bolting Tech. Prod. v. U.S. Fid. & Guar. Co. (E.D. Pa. 1996), 942 F.Supp. 1029, 1036, affd. (3d Cir. 1997), 118 F.3d 1574. If, prior to the inception of the Policy (i.e., September 25, 2000), Prime faxed ads whose content was similar to ads sent to Appellants, the "first publication" exclusion bars coverage for the Judgment.
Travelers has not had the opportunity to conduct discovery regarding the facts surrounding the Judgment or those relevant to the applicability of the "first publication" exclusion. Travelers requested in the alternative that the trial court deny Appellants' motion for summary judgment "to permit ... discovery to be had." Civ.R. 56(F). If this Court does not affirm the trial court's decision, it should remand the case so that Travelers has the opportunity to conduct discovery.

ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR II: THE TRIAL COURT CORRECTLY DENIED APPELLANTS' MOTION FOR RELIEF FROM JUDGMENT PURSUANT TO CIV.R. 60(B) BECAUSE THAT MOTION MERELY SOUGHT RECONSIDERATION OF THE TRIAL COURT'S FINRAL JUDGMENT.
Appellants' Civ.R. 60(B) motion asked the trial court to "reconsider and reverse" its decision. Appellants offered no new facts or arguments. Instead, they merely made the same arguments that the court had already rejected and claimed the court's decision was wrong. The trial court correctly denied Appellants' motion because it sought only reconsideration of the merits of the trial court's final judgment, and neither Civ.R. 60(B) nor any other rule permits a party to seek reconsideration of the merits of a final judgment. Kelly, 2007 Ohio App. LEXIS 5472, ** 10; Morley, 2004 Ohio App. LEXIS 4814, at ** 6; Smith, 1993 Ohio App. LEXIS 3467, at *12; Kerstetter, 91 Ohio App.3d at 602; Wohlabaugh, 2005 Ohio App. LEXIS 1174, at ** 8.
CONCLUSION
Based on the foregoing, this Court should affirm the trial court's orders granting summary judgment in favor of Travelers and denying Appellants' Civ.R. 60(B) motion.

Accordingly, the following is intended to restate the Courts oral decision.
Briefly stated, these claims arise from ACS Systems' use of DataMart Information Systems to send unsolicited advertising by fax to persons who did not wish to receive those communications, allegedly in violation of the federal Telephone Consumer Protection Act of 1991 ("TCPA"). A class action suit filed in 2000 called Kaufman v. ACS Systems, Inc., LASC case no. BC222588, sought injunctive and statutory remedies for this conduct. ACS sought coverage for defense of the Kaufman case from St. Paul, its insurer, who refused on the ground that there was no possibility of coverage, and it owed no duty to defend.
The Court Is persuaded by defendant's arguments that there is no potential for coverage under either the personal injury/property damage or the advertising injury rationales, as articulated in the First and Second Causes of Action. This conclusion has several components.

As a matter of law, It appears that there has been no "event" or "accident" of the type necessary to trigger coverage. This situation does not present an unintentional act; rather, everything about it involves Intentional acts by persons acting at the Instruction of and on behalf of ACS. The sending of the fax messages with this particular content to particular recipients at specific telephone numbers was exactly what was intended. The exact persons to whom the faxes were Intended to be directed received them; the only "fortuity" was that the persons to whom the faxes were directed didn't want them. This is not the type of "accident" which triggers coverage under the policy,
The Court is also not persuaded that these circumstances fall within the definition of "advertising injury," and more specifically, that the acts constitute "making known to any person or organization written or spoken material that violates an individual's right to privacy." The right to privacy-whether as a matter of federal constitutional law, Califomia constitutional law, or California common law-does not encompass the offense allegedly committed here. The conduct here does not appear to have been tortious or wrongful in any sense prior to the enactment of the TCPA. Indeed, the reason the federal statute was Invoked in the Kaufman sult Is because It explicitly prohibits conduct which previously had been permissible.'
